validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE/STATUS: the underlying agreement is real, not a phantom entry. RFE/RL (12 May 2007, 'Central Asia: Russian, Turkmen, Kazakh Leaders Agree On Caspian Pipeline') is a contemporaneous, independent report of Putin/Berdymukhammedov/Nazarbaev's trilateral declaration to build a gas pipeline along the Caspian coast from Turkmenistan via Kazakhstan to Russia. Jamestown ('Turkmenistan, Natural Gas, and the West') independently corroborates the 12 Dec 2007 draft-agreement signing and the Belek->Alexandrov Gay route. CACI Analyst (8 Apr 2009, 'Moscow and Ashgabat Fail To Agree over the Caspian Coastal Pipeline') documents the deal stalling through 2008-2009 as gas prices crashed. Critically, Eurasianet ('Turkmenistan: Russia Suspends Gas Supplies', 4 Jan 2016) — a source with NO connection to GEM, published 6+ years after the sheet's CancelledYear — states in a retrospective that 'the promised pipeline never got built,' which is fresh, independent, working confirmation that cancelled/never-revived remains correct as of 2016, with no later evidence of revival found in any subsequent search (TAPI, Central Asia-China, and East-West pipeline coverage from 2015-2020 never mention a Caspian coastal revival). Verdict: 'cancelled' stands, corroborated by 2 independent sources (RFE/RL 2007 for the agreement's existence; Eurasianet 2016 for confirmed non-completion), tier=high.

validity.researcher_notes: CLASSIFICATION nuance not visible from the sheet: CACI Analyst (8 Apr 2009) states the 'Caspian Coastal Pipeline (CCP, also called by its Russian name the Prikaspii)... is part of the western branch of the Central Asia-Center (CAC) pipeline, a spidery network inherited from the Soviet era,' 'constructed over a third of a century ago,' and reportedly still carrying ~2 bcm/y (in disrepair) as of the article date after being 're-opened in the middle of the current decade' (i.e. mid-2000s). So this is NOT a wholly greenfield line: an existing, decades-old physical pipe already occupied this corridor before the 2007 agreement. The 2007-2010 story that GEM tracks (Belek->Alexandrov Gay, 20-30 bcm/y target, cancelled 2010) is specifically the REFURBISHMENT/CAPACITY-EXPANSION project layered onto that old line (CACI: 'this would include an upgrade of the existing CCP where feasible... [plus] construction of an offshore pipeline to carry an additional 10 bcm/y'). 'Cancelled' is the right verdict for that expansion — it never proceeded past agreements/declarations, confirmed by Eurasianet's 'never got built.' But if the GEM row is implicitly meant to describe the whole named corridor rather than just the increment, a reader could wrongly infer no pipe exists on this route at all, when in fact a legacy Soviet-era line reportedly continued operating (at reduced volume) on the same alignment. This project's roster (P0740, P0761) doesn't include a separate 'Central Asia-Center' entity to check for a duplicate/overlap directly — routing this as a classification flag rather than resolving it here.

validity.researcher_notes: Two independent, contemporaneous sources name the SAME three ownership parties and only three: RFE/RL (12 May 2007) reports the trilateral talks were between Russia, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, with an accompanying (SEPARATE) deal to upgrade Uzbekistan infrastructure — explicitly NOT part of this pipeline agreement. CACI Analyst (8 Apr 2009) names the December-2007 signatories as 'the three main national trusts (respectively Gazprom, Turkmengaz, and KazMunaiGaz)'. Neither source, nor Jamestown, mentions Uzbekneftegaz as a party or owner of this project — Uzbekistan's involvement in the region (per RFE/RL) was a distinct, accompanying deal to upgrade Uzbek Soviet-era infrastructure on the CAC's eastern branch, not an ownership stake in the Caspian Coastal line. The sheet's Owner3='Uzbekneftegaz' looks like a conflation with that separate Uzbek infrastructure deal or with the broader CAC system (which does transit Uzbekistan). Separately, Owner1 (Gazprom) is recorded at 100% despite 3-4 named co-owners on the row — internally inconsistent; no source supports a single 100% holder, and the two independent sources instead describe three roughly co-equal national companies. Not resolved here since it requires an editorial decision (drop Uzbekneftegaz vs. verify further), staged as a concern rather than an applied edit per standing rules.

validity.researcher_notes: The recorded Capacity (25.00 bcm/y) does not clearly match any single figure in the primary reporting, and the underlying figures conflict across the plan's own history. CACI Analyst (8 Apr 2009) reports Putin's original 2007 proposal as 'a pipeline to carry 30 bcm/y along the land route, of which the first stage... would foresee at least 10 bcm/y that Russia would commit to purchase,' PLUS a separate 'offshore pipeline to carry an additional 10 bcm/y.' Jamestown corroborates the 10 bcm/y first-stage purchase commitment specifically ('up to 10 billion cubic meters of Turkmen gas annually'). So the sourced numbers are 10 (near-term commitment), 30 (announced land-route target), and up to 40 (land+offshore) bcm/y — not 25. The 20-30 bcm/y range (and the sheet's apparent midpoint of that range) appears in later secondary/aggregator summaries but I could not find an independent primary source stating 25 bcm/y specifically; the figure looks like an unsourced smoothing of a range rather than a corroborated data point. Flagging as a material spec disagreement rather than silently passing it; not forcing a replacement number since none of the individually-cited figures (10/30/40) is unambiguously 'the' right one for a single Capacity field either.
